A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AudioTrust and retain the same core benchmark. Their main texts, tables, figures, equations, and complete appendices support comparison; visual inspection resolved extraction problems in dense tables.

before.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of nine ALLMs across six trustworthiness dimensions in Tables 1–6, with detailed results and analyses in the appendices.

after.justification: v3 reports original evaluations of fourteen ALLMs, revised privacy and authentication results, and human validation of automated assessments.

M1.justification: The benchmark's core audio-construction procedures and decoupled inference/evaluation architecture in Appendix C remain intact. No new model architecture, training objective, attack-generation algorithm, or model inference method is introduced; changes concern evaluation and validation.

E1.justification: The six benchmark dimensions and their principal datasets, attributes, and domains are retained. However, v2's authentication task requiring selection between two speakers is removed from v3's protocols and reported results (Appendix I.3–I.5; v2 Table 25 versus v3 Table 27).

E2.justification: Tables 1–6 expand the evaluated roster from nine to fourteen ALLMs by adding Step-Fun, Qwen2.5-Omni, Kimi-Audio, OpenS2S, and Step-Audio2. Qwen2.5-Omni was mentioned in v2, but did not participate in these reported comparisons.

E3.justification: Privacy refusal changes from scores 4–5 to 3–5, and the age-evaluation prompt is substantially revised (G.3–G.4). Hybrid-spoofing judging changes to whether the user's goal was fulfilled (I.3). v3 also introduces emotional prefixes for the text safety control, sampled human validation, and an explicit minimum of ten leaked samples for conditional accuracy reporting.

E4.justification: v3 adds a human check of evaluator reliability (C) and refines the audio-versus-text safety analysis with emotion-augmented text (F.5). It removes the speaker-preference analysis (I.5). Existing gender/emotion comparisons, robustness analyses, background-audio controls, and stricter authentication-prompt comparisons largely remain.

E5.justification: Appendix C adds a sampled estimate of human–automated agreement: 10% of data, twenty annotators, three independent reviews per item, and majority voting. v2 had expert scoring but no corresponding platform-wide agreement estimate. Neither version provides repeated-seed uncertainty or confidence intervals; table subscripts generally indicate differences from averages.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive results for five models, revises fairness and privacy values, expands leakage-accuracy reporting, and removes speaker-preference results. GPT-4o Audio's hybrid-spoofing FAR changes from 10% to 0% in Table 6 under a revised judging procedure, so this is not an established same-setting improvement. Many retained hallucination scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulations, including group unfairness, hallucination metrics, DSR/HRR, CM-WER, and CCR, remain substantively unchanged. Neither version introduces theoretical propositions or proofs. Revised empirical scoring thresholds and prompts do not add mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains a comprehensive six-dimensional AudioTrust benchmark. v3 adds explicit headline claims that non-semantic acoustic cues manipulate model behavior and that human validation supports automated assessment reliability. The underlying benchmark contribution and broad deployment conclusions are retained.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantial mechanistic interpretations: over-textualization, insufficient attention to paralinguistic information during training, stronger front-end processing as an explanation for proprietary-model robustness, and differences between human commonsense and model reasoning. It also adds a dual-use discussion. These extend scientific interpretation beyond v2's model-performance summaries; Appendix K's limitations remain essentially unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 adds a reproducibility statement describing scripts, metadata, configurations, and an additional repository address. It documents validation staffing and sampling, emotional text prefixes, and more explicit evaluator response handling. Most existing generation recipes, example inputs, and public dataset access information are retained; resource availability itself cannot be verified from the PDFs.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for newer audio models, private-attribute profiling, location leakage, and robustness. It removes the ASVspoof references previously grounding the authentication taxonomy. Appendix J and the central positioning against capability-focused and narrowly scoped safety benchmarks remain largely unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and Sections 2–7 are extensively rewritten, replacing many research-question lists and model summaries with explanations centered on acoustic risks. Terminology and citation style change, and reproducibility, ethics, and LLM-usage statements are added.

P2.justification: Figures 1–3 update model rosters and the leaderboard, and the main tables expand. Appendix fairness and safety tables are split by model openness; privacy tables gain accuracy and leakage-denominator columns; authentication tables are reoriented. These substantial display changes accompany document-wide header, typography, and placement changes.

improvement.justification: The expanded model comparisons, human validation (C), emotion-augmented text control (F.5), and conditional leakage analysis strengthen the evidence. However, revised reporting introduces unresolved inconsistencies: v3 Table 4 gives GPT-4o mini Audio an inference refusal rate of 10.50%, while Table 18's 9%, 33%, and 0% across three equally sized categories imply 14%. v2's corresponding sum was consistent. These discrepancies, alongside changed scoring procedures and stronger mechanistic interpretations, prevent a reliable judgment of net quality improvement.
